title: Sepsis and septic shock: initial management
subject: critical-care
summary: Early recognition, cultures, antimicrobials within 1 hour for suspected septic shock or probable sepsis, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypoperfusion, noradrenaline to a MAP of 65 mmHg, and urgent source control.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Sepsis: life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection (acute SOFA score rise of 2 or more points).
Septic shock: sepsis needing vasopressors to keep MAP at or above 65 mmHg AND lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
Do not use qSOFA alone as a screening tool; it is specific but not sensitive. Use it with NEWS2, SIRS criteria and clinical judgement.
Hypoperfusion clues: hypotension, lactate 4 mmol/L or more, prolonged capillary refill, mottling, reduced urine output, altered mentation.

sections.title: First hour
items: Measure lactate; re-measure within 2 to 4 hours if the first value is above 2 mmol/L and use the trend to guide resuscitation.
Take blood cultures (at least 2 sets) and site-specific cultures before antimicrobials, provided this does not delay treatment.
Probable sepsis or possible septic shock: give broad-spectrum IV antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 hour of recognition.
Possible sepsis without shock: rapid assessment for infective versus non-infective causes; if concern for infection persists, give antimicrobials within 3 hours.

Hypotension or lactate 4 mmol/L or more: give at least 30 mL/kg IV balanced crystalloid (Ringer lactate or Plasma-Lyte preferred over 0.9% saline) within the first 3 hours, reassessing after each bolus. With BMI above 30, calculate the volume on adjusted or ideal body weight.
Start noradrenaline if MAP stays below 65 mmHg during or after fluids. A peripheral cannula in a large proximal vein is acceptable while central access is arranged; do not delay vasopressors.

sections.title: Investigations
items: CBC, renal and liver function, electrolytes, glucose, coagulation profile, arterial or venous blood gas with lactate.
Blood cultures x 2, urine culture, sputum or other site cultures as indicated; procalcitonin may help decide when to stop antibiotics but not when to start.
Imaging to find a source needing control: chest X-ray, point-of-care ultrasound, CT abdomen as indicated.

sections.title: Antimicrobials and source control
items: Choose the empiric regimen by suspected source, recent antibiotic exposure, healthcare contact and the local antibiogram (see the Antibiogram tab and ICMR treatment guidelines).
Add MRSA cover only when MRSA risk is high. Use two gram-negative agents only for patients at high risk of multidrug-resistant organisms.
For beta-lactams, use prolonged infusion for maintenance dosing after the initial bolus.
Identify or exclude an anatomical source needing drainage, debridement or device removal and control it early, ideally within 6 hours of diagnosis (SSC 2026); sooner is better when feasible.
Reassess daily for de-escalation; prefer shorter courses with adequate source control.

sections.title: Haemodynamic and adjunctive care
items: Target an initial MAP of 65 mmHg; at age 65 or older an initial MAP of 60 to 65 mmHg is suggested over higher targets (SSC 2026). Guide further fluids by dynamic measures (passive leg raise, stroke volume or pulse pressure variation) and capillary refill time rather than static CVP alone.

SSC 2026 suggests crystalloids alone rather than crystalloids plus supplemental albumin (conditional, moderate certainty), a change from 2021; albumin is not routine. It may still have a selected role after large crystalloid volumes or in cirrhosis; avoid it in traumatic brain injury. Avoid starches and gelatin.
Add vasopressin 0.03 units/min when noradrenaline reaches 0.25 to 0.5 mcg/kg/min, rather than escalating noradrenaline alone.
Cardiac dysfunction with persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate MAP and volume: add dobutamine or switch to adrenaline.
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV (50 mg every 6 hours) when noradrenaline or adrenaline of 0.25 mcg/kg/min or more has been needed for at least 4 hours.
Start insulin when blood glucose is 180 mg/dL (10 mmol/L) or higher; target 144 to 180 mg/dL.
Transfuse red cells at haemoglobin below 7 g/dL in most adults.
Give pharmacological VTE prophylaxis (LMWH preferred) and stress ulcer prophylaxis in patients with GI bleeding risk factors. Do not give IV vitamin C.

sections.title: Monitoring and targets
items: MAP 65 mmHg or more (60 to 65 mmHg acceptable at age 65 or older), urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h or more, falling lactate, capillary refill time normalising.
Invasive arterial monitoring as soon as practical for patients on vasopressors.
Sepsis-induced ARDS: tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O.

sections.title: Escalate to ICU
items: Any vasopressor requirement, lactate 4 mmol/L or more after fluids, rising oxygen requirement, reduced consciousness or new organ failure.
Admit to ICU within 6 hours for patients who need intensive care.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Waiting for cultures or imaging before the first antimicrobial dose in suspected shock.
Repeated fluid boluses without reassessment in patients with heart failure, ARDS or oligo-anuric AKI.
Missing a drainable source (obstructed kidney, cholangitis, empyema, abscess, necrotising soft tissue infection).

drugs.name: Balanced crystalloid (Ringer lactate)
drugs.dose: At least 30 mL/kg IV within the first 3 hours for hypotension or lactate 4 mmol/L or more
drugs.notes: Give in boluses of 250 to 500 mL with reassessment after each. BMI above 30: use adjusted or ideal body weight.

drugs.name: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine)
drugs.dose: Start 0.05 to 0.1 mcg/kg/min IV, titrate to MAP 65 mmHg

drugs.name: Vasopressin
drugs.notes: Add when noradrenaline is 0.25 to 0.5 mcg/kg/min.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.notes: Septic shock with ongoing vasopressor need of 0.25 mcg/kg/min or more for 4 hours.
